<x_0.7383><y_0.0>**Chap. II.** _Source of_ _Wealth._<x_0.9326><y_0.0625><class_Caption>

<x_0.126><y_0.0305>**CHAP.II.** _Of the Sources of Wealth._<x_0.6807><y_0.0539><class_Section-header>

<x_0.0078><y_0.0586>ALL wealth arifes from three fources; it is either produced by the fpontaneous bounty of nature, or it is the fruit of human indultry, or it is generated by the judicious employment of a quantity of wealth previously accumulated. To thefe three heads then of _land, la-bour_, and _capital_, all national wealth may be re-ferred.<x_0.7998><y_0.1625><class_Text>

<x_0.0127><y_0.1609>Smith has treated of the revenue derived from thefe three fources as forming the constituent parts of the price of commodities; and with regard to labour in particular, repeatedly confiders it as the only fource of wealth\*. According to the view, however, given above, the price of all commodities depends entirely on the proportion between the demand and the supply. Labour, therefore, (and the fame may be laid of land and capi-tal), is only a means of furnishing or increasing a lupply of thofe articles for which there already exilisa demand, and unlefs it be fuccefslul in lo doing, the moft levere labours will meet with no remuneration whatever. We shall therefore proceed to consider the revenue which arises from thefe different fources, and the circumstances by which it is increased or diminished.<x_0.8008><y_0.3766><class_Text>

<x_0.8135><y_0.2211>Book i. cb. v. vi. via<x_0.9336><y_0.2492><class_Caption>

<x_0.2852><y_0.3805>SECT. I. _Land._<x_0.5195><y_0.3984><class_Section-header>

<x_0.0215><y_0.3977>All land which is not naturally barren, and is cultivated with any cafe, affords something more than is necellary to pay the expense of labouring it. This furplus goes as a rent to the landlord, who, in confidera-tion of receiving it without rifk or trouble, relinquifies to the farmer the profits of cultivation.<x_0.8076><y_0.4883><class_Text>

<x_0.0225><y_0.4844>The proportion of the produce of a field which is to go for rent, varies with different circumstances. The chief of thefe is the fertility of the foil, the extent of the market, which enables the produce to be difpofed of to greater advantage, the profperity or poverty of the country, which causes a greater or less demand for that produce, and the average fill and activity of the farmers, which will enable them to turn the fertility of the ground to better account. It is almost needless to obferve, were it not for the vague language often made ufe of upon this subject, that the rate at which farms let, mult, like all other commodities, depend altogether upon the demand and the lupply. If much is to be made by farming, many will bid for farms, and the rent will be railed by their competition, and _vice verfu._ The idea that all the landlords of an extensive country may combine to raife their rents, is altogether chimeri-cal. Even could it take place, it could be accomplished only by a certain number of them allowing their lands to lie wafte, which, diminishing the lupply, would doubtlefs raife the rent of the cultivated lands. But we need not fear that any landlord should leave his lands in this condition, from a culpable scheme of agrandizing the reft of his body at his own expence, as well as that of the public.<x_0.8174><y_0.843><class_Text>

<x_0.0342><y_0.8391>Land which produces food for man will at all times afford rent to the landlord, in proportion to its fertility, and the other circumstances mentioned above. Men multiply in proportion to the means of fubifference; they have even a constant tendency to multiply beyond the means; hence there is always a full demand for this species<x_0.8184><y_0.9445><class_Text>
